newsitem.title: USA: ValuJet handlers didn't view oxygen tanks a danger.
newsitem.headline: ValuJet handlers didn't view oxygen tanks a danger.

text.p: Two ramp agents who loaded oxygen canisters onto a doomed ValuJet flight said Tuesday they had no idea they were putting hazardous materials on the plane that were later suspected of causing a disastrous fire.

The testimony came on the second day of a National Transportation Safety Board hearing into the May 11 crash of the ValuJet DC-9, which plunged into Florida's Everglades shortly after take-off from Miami International Airport, killing all 110 people on board.

At the opening of the hearing Monday, investigators released transcripts of cockpit recordings that documented the final, frantic moments of the flight, during which a passenger shouted "We're on fire" and a flight attendant cried for oxygen as chaos erupted in the passenger cabin.

Testimony Tuesday centred on the loading of five boxes of oxygen generators aboard the plane. The canisters, each about the size of a tennis ball container, are suspected of either starting or feeding a ferocious fire that began in the forward cargo hold and spread to the passenger compartment.
The two agents testified about a chain of events that could have contributed to the fire.

Christopher Ramkissoon, a lead ramp agent who oversaw the loading, said he had been trained not to load hazardous material onto ValuJet aircraft but saw no warning labels on the boxes. "They were oxygen canisters, marked empty. The boxes didn't have a label on it saying 'hazardous material.'"
Ramkissoon, who had been working for ValuJet for six months at the time of the crash, said he would not have permitted the boxes on board if they had "hazmat" labels.

He named "oxygen bottles" as one of the hazardous materials he knew should not be shipped on ValuJet planes but said he did not question whether the oxygen generators, listed as "oxy canisters empty" on the shipping ticket, should be loaded.

Ramkissoon said he trusted the shippers would know what to ship and would pack it properly. "I believe in them that they would prepare them the right way for shipping," he said. "When I saw 'empty' right off, it meant empty," he said in answer to a question about whether he should have loaded the canisters.
His testimony appeared to outline another in a series of events that led to the oxygen canisters being loaded in violation of federal and airline regulations.

Dennis Segarra, the ValuJet ramp agent who stacked the boxes inside the cargo hold, said he stored the canisters securely although he said one box appeared to be packed loosely and he was able to hear a clinking sound within.
He said, like Ramkissoon, that there were no warning labels on the boxes.

On Monday, officials from SabreTech Corp., the maintenance contractor that removed the canisters from other ValuJet planes, conceded that mechanics failed to install safety caps designed to prevent them from firing accidentally and mislabeled them as empty.
